i18n.en: Woe, land of the rustling of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Cush,
i18n.he: ה֥וֹי אֶ֖רֶץ צִלְצַ֣ל כְּנָפָ֑יִם אֲשֶׁ֥ר מֵעֵ֖בֶר לְנַֽהֲרֵי־כֽוּשׁ׃

notes.official:
*Ṣilṣal kᵉnāp̄āyim* is the crux of the chapter. *Ṣilṣal* is a reduplicated noun of the sound-imitating root *ṣll* “to tingle, quiver, whir.” The same consonants name a whirring locust at Deut 28:42 and a fish-spear at Job 40:31, and the plural *ṣelṣᵉlîm* are “cymbals” (2 Sam 6:5; Ps 150:5). *Kᵉnāp̄āyim* is the dual of *kānāp̄* “wing,” a word that also means “edge, extremity” and “skirt of a garment.” The line keeps ASV “the land of the rustling of wings” (JPS 1917 “the buzzing of wings”; Koren “buzzing wings”), translates the dual simply as “wings,” and supplies no referent (overlay `tziltzal-kenafayim-whirring-wings-isaiah-18`).

The proposed readings, with their sources:
- **A sound of wings, usually insects.** BDB s.v. *ṣilṣāl* gives “land of buzzing of (insects’) wings (so prob.),” and BDB s.v. *kānāp̄* refers the phrase to the swarms of flies of the Nile lands, possibly the tsetse fly (after Duhm and Cheyne). Compare the “fly … of the rivers of Egypt” at 7:18.
- **The noise of an army.** BDB records this as the view of Gesenius’s *Thesaurus*.
- **Shadow.** This reading connects *ṣilṣal* with *ṣēl* “shade.” KJV has “the land shadowing with wings.” BDB records that Knobel and Dillmann took it of the tropical sun, which casts shadows both north and south. NJPS has “land in the deep shadow of wings,” with the note “Or ‘Most sheltered land’” and cross-references to 30:2–3 and Ps 36:8; 57:2; 61:5.
- **Sails.** The LXX reads οὐαὶ γῆς πλοίων πτέρυγες, “woe to the land, wings of ships,” and so takes the wings as sails, in keeping with the boats of 18:2. BDB judges that a reference to sails “would be suitable, but *ṣilṣal* does not favour this.”

NRSV “whirring wings” is not verified.

*Kûš* is “Cush” (overlay `cush-names-isaiah`): the Nile lands south of Egypt, ancient Nubia. Most commentators connect the oracle with the Kushite (Twenty-fifth) Dynasty, which ruled Egypt in Isaiah’s lifetime. ASV and JPS 1917 have “Ethiopia,” after the LXX Αἰθιοπίας, and NJPS has “Nubia.” *Mēʿēḇer lᵉnahărê-ḵûš* is “beyond the rivers of Cush” (ASV, JPS 1917, NJPS). The same phrase opens Zeph 3:10, where NJPS notes that the thought recalls Isa 18:1, 7. *Hôy* is “Woe” (overlay `hoy-woe-isaiah`), in the vocative, as at 10:5; ASV, JPS 1917 and NJPS have “Ah,” and KJV has “Woe.” *ʾEreṣ* is the territorial “land” (central `eretz`).

**Wheel of Heaven reading (reception note, not a translation claim; claim type: speculative).** The canon does not cite Isa 18. *The Book Which Tells the Truth* quotes the six wings of the seraphim at Isa 6:2 and reads them as “an autonomous suit fitted with six small thrusters” (TBWTT 3:144–145). That is the only passage in which the canon reads wings in Isaiah as devices. Outside Isaiah, the closest canon parallel is LWTE 2:187–190, which quotes the locusts of Rev 9:7–10 (“the sound of their wings was as the sound of chariots”) and reads them as metal aircraft: “the noise comes from the jet engines,” and the missiles are “tucked under their wings.” That passage concerns human aircraft dropping atomic bombs in a future war (LWTE 2:184). It does not concern Isa 18. To read the “whirring of wings” of 18:1 as the sound of flying craft would extend that reading to a verse the canon does not discuss. The Hebrew does not require it: the lexica connect *ṣilṣal* with insects, and the next verse puts the envoys in papyrus boats on the water. The note is here only so that the reach of the lens can be audited. The line and the glossary carry only the Hebrew wording.

notes.official:
*Gôy qaw-qāw ûmᵉḇûsāh* is the hardest phrase in the verse (overlay `qav-qav-line-isaiah`). *Qaw* is the measuring line (2 Kgs 21:13; Isa 34:11, 17; 44:13), and *mᵉḇûsāh* is a “trampling” (*bws*). The line keeps the ASV reading, modernized: “a nation that measures out and treads down” (ASV “meteth out and treadeth down”; KJV “meted out and trodden down”). BDB, however, reads *qawqāw* “might (?)” and says that most interpreters do the same, comparing Arabic *quwwa* “strength”: “a mighty nation.” JPS 1917 “sturdy” and Koren “mighty and conquering” follow that view. NJPS has “a nation of gibber and chatter,” with the note “Meaning of Heb. uncertain; cf. 28.10,” because distant nations are often described by their unintelligible speech (33:19; Deut 28:49; Jer 5:15). The LXX has ἀνέλπιστον “without hope,” which derives the word from *qwh* “to hope,” and it reads *qaw lāqāw* at 28:10, 13 the same way (ἐλπίδα ἐπ’ ἐλπίδι). The two passages should be translated consistently. ASV takes both from “line” (28:10, 13 “line upon line”).

*Mᵉmuššāḵ ûmôrāṭ* (also 18:7). *Mᵉmuššāḵ* is the Pual of *mšk* “draw out,” which BDB glosses “of persons, = tall.” *Môrāṭ* is the Pual of *mrṭ* “make bare, smooth, polish.” The verb is used of a polished sword (Ezek 21:14–16) and of plucked hair (Ezra 9:3). The line keeps ASV “tall and smooth” and does not decide whether the sense is smooth-skinned or shaven. JPS 1917 has “tall and of glossy skin,” KJV “scattered and peeled,” and NJPS “far and remote … thrust forth and away” (“Meaning of Heb. uncertain”). Herodotus (3.20), often cited here, calls the Ethiopians the tallest and most handsome of men. Compare the Sabeans, “men of stature,” at 45:14.

The other phrases of the verse:
- *ʿam nôrāʾ min-hûʾ wāhālᵊʾāh* is literally “a people feared from it and onward.” The line takes it in time, “from their beginning onward,” with ASV and JPS 1917 (KJV “hitherto”). It uses “feared” for the Niphal participle of *yrʾ*, where ASV has “terrible.” A sense in space (“far and wide”) is also possible.
- *Bāzᵉʾû* occurs only here and in 18:7. BDB glosses it “divide, cut through,” comparing Aramaic *bᵉzaʿ* “cleave,” so “whose land the rivers divide” (ASV, JPS 1917). KJV has “have spoiled” and NJPS “is cut off by streams.”
- *Ṣîrîm* are “envoys” (BDB: “envoy, from Cush Is 18:2”; ASV “ambassadors”). *Bayyām* “by the sea” may mean the Nile, which is called *yām* at 19:5, but the line does not identify the water.
- *Kᵉlê-ḡōmeʾ* are “vessels of papyrus” (ASV, JPS 1917; BDB “vessels of paper-reed”), the reed of the basket in Exod 2:3. The LXX has ἐπιστολὰς βυβλίνας “papyrus letters.”
- NJPS notes that the masculine participle *haššōlēaḥ* “which sends” agrees with “nation,” not with the feminine “land” of 18:1. The English relative leaves the antecedent open.
- The imperative *lᵉḵû malʾāḵîm qallîm* “Go, you swift messengers” has no introduction in the Hebrew. ASV supplies “[saying],” and NJPS reorders the verse. The line supplies nothing (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-18`).

notes.official:
*Šôp̄ār* is “a shofar”: the line now uses the corpus form under central `shofar-rams-horn-signal-instrument-cross-corpus`, which transliterates the word in every context and reserves “trumpet” for the metal *ḥăṣōṣᵉrāh*. The Translator had “a trumpet.” ASV has “the trumpet,” JPS 1917 “the horn,” NJPS “a ram’s horn,” Koren “a shofar” and the LXX σάλπιγγος. By founder ruling of 2026-11-26 the stable 27:13 now prints “a great shofar” as well (chapter 27 version 1.0.1; overlay `shofar-gadol-ingathering-isaiah-27`).

*Kinśōʾ-nēs hārîm* is “when a signal is raised on the mountains” (overlay `nes-signal-isaiah`; ASV and JPS 1917 “ensign,” NJPS “flag”). Neither infinitive names its subject. KJV and Koren supply “he” for both (“when he lifteth up an ensign … when he bloweth a trumpet”). The line keeps the impersonal construction. *Tirʾû … tišmāʿû* are imperfects, rendered as imperatives (“see … hear!”) with ASV and NJPS; a future, “you will see … you will hear,” is also possible (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-18`). *Yōšᵉḇê ṯēḇēl wᵉšōḵnê ʾāreṣ* pairs “the world” with “the earth.” The universal sense takes “earth” (overlay `eretz-cosmic-scope-isaiah-24`). NJPS opens the verse with “[Say this:],” which turns it into the message of the envoys of 18:2. The line adds no such words.

paragraphs.translit: kol-yōšəbē tēbēl wəšōkənē ʾāreṣ kinśōʾ-nēs hārīm tirʾū wəkitqōaʿ šōpār tišmāʿū (s)

paragraphs.text: כִּי֩ כֹ֨ה אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֵלַ֔י אשקוטה [אֶשְׁקֳטָ֖ה] וְאַבִּ֣יטָה בִמְכוֹנִ֑י כְּחֹ֥ם צַח֙ עֲלֵי־א֔וֹר כְּעָ֥ב טַ֖ל בְּחֹ֥ם קָצִֽיר׃

i18n.en: For thus YHWH has said to me: I will be quiet, and I will look on in my dwelling place, like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.
i18n.he: כִּי֩ כֹ֨ה אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֵלַ֔י אשקוטה [אֶשְׁקֳטָ֖ה] וְאַבִּ֣יטָה בִמְכוֹנִ֑י כְּחֹ֥ם צַח֙ עֲלֵי־א֔וֹר כְּעָ֥ב טַ֖ל בְּחֹ֥ם קָצִֽיר׃

notes.official:
The ketiv אשקוטה and the qere *ʾešqᵒṭāh* are the same form, “I will be quiet,” the cohortative of *šqṭ*. They differ only in the full spelling of the vowel, and the line reads the qere (overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`). YHWH’s stillness is that of a watcher waiting for the moment to strike (18:5). The messenger formula introduces the divine speech without quotation marks (overlay `title-and-meta-conventions-isaiah`).

The two similes are uncertain, and the line keeps ASV (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-18`):
- *Kᵉḥōm ṣaḥ ʿălê-ʾôr* is “like clear heat in sunshine” (ASV, JPS 1917). KJV has “like a clear heat upon herbs” and NJPS “like a scorching heat upon sprouts.” Both take *ʾôr* as “herb,” the sense KJV gives *ʾôrōṯ* at 26:19 (“the dew of herbs”), which the book prints as “dew of lights.”
- *Kᵉʿāḇ ṭal* is “like a cloud of dew.” *Ṭal* is the night mist (BDB “night-mist, taking place of our dew”). NJPS has “a rain-cloud,” with the note “I.e., like a threat of disaster; cf. Eccl. 11.4.”

*Wᵉʾabbîṭāh bimḵônî* is “and I will look on in my dwelling place” (ASV “behold,” JPS 1917 “look on”). NJPS “I rest calm and confident” takes *hibbîṭ* as “rely” (Job 6:19). *Bᵉḥōm qāṣîr* is “in the heat of harvest.” The LXX has ἡμέρας ἀμήτου “of the day of harvest,” which presupposes *bᵉyôm*. Whether 1QIsaᵃ has this reading was not verified. The line keeps MT.

paragraphs.translit: kī kōh ʾāmar YHWH ʾēlay ʾšqwṭh [ʾešqŏṭāh] wəʾabbīṭāh bimkōnī kəḥōm ṣaḥ ʿălē-ʾōr kəʿāb ṭal bəḥōm qāṣīr

paragraphs.text: כִּֽי־לִפְנֵ֤י קָצִיר֙ כְּתָם־פֶּ֔רַח וּבֹ֥סֶר גֹּמֵ֖ל יִֽהְיֶ֣ה נִצָּ֑ה וְכָרַ֤ת הַזַּלְזַלִּים֙ בַּמַּזְמֵר֔וֹת וְאֶת־הַנְּטִישׁ֖וֹת הֵסִ֥יר הֵתַֽז׃

i18n.en: For before the harvest, when the blossom is over and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he will cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and the spreading branches he will take away, he will cut down.
i18n.he: כִּֽי־לִפְנֵ֤י קָצִיר֙ כְּתָם־פֶּ֔רַח וּבֹ֥סֶר גֹּמֵ֖ל יִֽהְיֶ֣ה נִצָּ֑ה וְכָרַ֤ת הַזַּלְזַלִּים֙ בַּמַּזְמֵר֔וֹת וְאֶת־הַנְּטִישׁ֖וֹת הֵסִ֥יר הֵתַֽז׃

notes.official: *Lip̄nê qāṣîr* “before the harvest” is MT. NJPS notes “Emendation yields ‘vintage’,” since the images are of the vine; the line keeps MT. *Bōser* is the unripe grape. *Zalzallîm* “sprigs, tendrils” occurs only here, and so does *hēṯaz* “cut down” (*tzz*). *Hēsîr hēṯaz* is two perfects without a conjunction: “he will take away, he will cut down.” ASV supplies “[and],” and the line keeps the Hebrew asyndeton (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-18`). The subject is unnamed. It is YHWH of 18:4, and the line leaves him unnamed, as does NJPS 1985 (“He”). NJPS reads the pruned branches as “a figure of speech for the defeated enemy.”

paragraphs.translit: kī-lipnē qāṣīr kətom-peraḥ ūbōser gōmēl yihyeh niṣṣāh wəkārat hazzalzallīm bammazmērōt wəʾet-hannəṭīšōt hēsīr hētaz

paragraphs.text: יֵעָזְב֤וּ יַחְדָּו֙ לְעֵ֣יט הָרִ֔ים וּֽלְבֶהֱמַ֖ת הָאָ֑רֶץ וְקָ֤ץ עָלָיו֙ הָעַ֔יִט וְכָל־בֶּהֱמַ֥ת הָאָ֖רֶץ עָלָ֥יו תֶּחֱרָֽף׃

i18n.en: They shall be left together to the ravenous birds of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth; and the ravenous birds shall summer upon them, and all the beasts of the earth shall winter upon them.
i18n.he: יֵעָזְב֤וּ יַחְדָּו֙ לְעֵ֣יט הָרִ֔ים וּֽלְבֶהֱמַ֖ת הָאָ֑רֶץ וְקָ֤ץ עָלָיו֙ הָעַ֔יִט וְכָל־בֶּהֱמַ֥ת הָאָ֖רֶץ עָלָ֥יו תֶּחֱרָֽף׃

notes.official:
*Bᵉhemaṯ hāʾāreṣ* is “the beasts of the earth” (ASV, JPS 1917, NJPS, Koren). The verse uses the carrion formula of the curses, in which the bodies of the slain are left to the birds and to “the beasts of the earth” (ASV Deut 28:26; Jer 7:33; corpus 1 Sam 17:46). In that idiom *ʾereṣ* is the ground on which the wild animals range, not a territory. The line therefore departs from the default “land” of central `eretz`, and a context clause covering the formula is proposed in the central diff.

*ʿÊṭ* is the bird of prey, taken collectively: “the ravenous birds” (ASV, JPS 1917). NJPS has “kites” and Koren “predatory birds.” The LXX has “the birds of the sky,” the form of the formula found elsewhere. *Qāṣ* “summer” and *teḥĕrāp̄* “winter” are denominative verbs from *qayiṣ* “summer” and *ḥōrep̄* “autumn, winter.” BDB glosses *teḥĕrāp̄* here “spend the harvest-time upon it.” The pair means that the carcasses lie through the whole year. *ʿĀlāyw* is singular (“upon it”), referring to the cut-down mass of 18:5, and the line has the plural with ASV (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-18`).

paragraphs.translit: yēʿāzəbū yaḥdāw ləʿēṭ hārīm ūləbehĕmat hāʾāreṣ wəqāṣ ʿālāyw hāʿayiṭ wəkol-behĕmat hāʾāreṣ ʿālāyw teḥĕrāp

paragraphs.text: בָּעֵת֩ הַהִ֨יא יֽוּבַל־שַׁ֜י לַיהוָ֣ה צְבָא֗וֹת עַ֚ם מְמֻשָּׁ֣ךְ וּמוֹרָ֔ט וּמֵעַ֥ם נוֹרָ֖א מִן־ה֣וּא וָהָ֑לְאָה גּ֣וֹי ׀ קַו־קָ֣ו וּמְבוּסָ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר בָּזְא֤וּ נְהָרִים֙ אַרְצ֔וֹ אֶל־מְק֛וֹם שֵׁם־יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת הַר־צִיּֽוֹן׃ (ס)

i18n.en: In that time a gift shall be brought to YHWH of hosts, a people tall and smooth, and from a people feared from their beginning onward, a nation that measures out and treads down, whose land the rivers divide, to the place of the name of YHWH of hosts, Mount Zion.
i18n.he: בָּעֵת֩ הַהִ֨יא יֽוּבַל־שַׁ֜י לַיהוָ֣ה צְבָא֗וֹת עַ֚ם מְמֻשָּׁ֣ךְ וּמוֹרָ֔ט וּמֵעַ֥ם נוֹרָ֖א מִן־ה֣וּא וָהָ֑לְאָה גּ֣וֹי ׀ קַו־קָ֣ו וּמְבוּסָ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר בָּזְא֤וּ נְהָרִים֙ אַרְצ֔וֹ אֶל־מְק֛וֹם שֵׁם־יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת הַר־צִיּֽוֹן׃ (ס)

notes.official:
MT reads *yûḇal-šay … ʿam mᵉmuššāḵ ûmôrāṭ ûmēʿam nôrāʾ*: “a gift shall be brought … a people tall and smooth, and from a people feared.” It has no preposition before the first “people,” which therefore stands in apposition to the gift, and “from” before the second. ASV (“[from] a people”) and NJPS (“[From] a people”) supply the preposition, and JPS 1917 has “of a people.” The LXX has ἐκ λαοῦ … καὶ ἀπὸ λαοῦ, “from a people … and from a people.” Whether 1QIsaᵃ has *mēʿam* was not verified. The line keeps MT (overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`). MT can be read as presenting the people themselves as the offering, as the nations bring Israel “as an offering” at 66:20. The supplied preposition makes them the bearers of the gift.

*Šay* is a “gift offered as homage” (BDB; Ps 68:30; 76:12): ASV and JPS 1917 “a present,” NJPS “tribute.” The epithets repeated from 18:2 are rendered the same way there and here (overlays `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-18`, `qav-qav-line-isaiah`). *ʾEl-mᵉqôm šēm-YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ* is literally “to the place of the name of YHWH of hosts.” It recalls Deuteronomy’s “the place which YHWH will choose … to put his name there” (Deut 12:5, 11). NJPS has “where the name … abides.” The verse reverses 18:2: the envoys sent out to the distant people are answered by that people’s gift at Mount Zion, a theme Zeph 3:10 takes up (“from beyond the rivers of Cush”).

paragraphs.translit: bāʿēt hahīʾ yūbal-šay laYHWH ṣəbāʾōt ʿam məmuššāk ūmōrāṭ ūmēʿam nōrāʾ min-hūʾ wāhāləʾāh gōy | qaw-qāw ūməbūsāh ʾăšer bāzəʾū nəhārīm ʾarṣō ʾel-məqōm šēm-YHWH ṣəbāʾōt har-ṣiyyōn (s)
